headline: A middleware that refuses a request now stops it, and the audit rows the framework promised are written for the first time
summary:
`b.router` invoked each `use()` middleware with a `next` callback and ignored the argument it was given. A middleware reporting failure the documented way, `next(err)`, was read as if it had called `next()`, so the request continued to the route handler and the response was produced as though the check had passed. Any authentication, authorization or CSRF middleware written to that contract was advisory: it could log a refusal and still serve the request. `b.testing.request` routed its own failures past the application's `onError`, which is why the framework's own harness could not see it.

The audit chain had a quieter version of the same problem. `b.audit` requires an action to be `namespace.verb[.qualifier]` in lowercase with a registered namespace, and `safeEmit` caught the refusal and returned, which is indistinguishable from the drop-silent contract it keeps for a sink on the request path. Thirty-nine emit sites across nineteen files passed an action the validator refuses, so each call reported success, raised nothing, and wrote no row: the record of an operator turning a content scanner off, the backup envelope key rotation auditors ask for, every 0-RTT decision, every differential-privacy budget decision, and the credential lifecycle of `b.auth.sdJwtVc`. Each action is corrected, and `b.audit.refusedActions()` now reports an action that was not recorded instead of absorbing it, which is what then found three further namespaces, `guardsql`, `fsm` and `worm`, whose rows were going nowhere either.

A request target recorded as a field carries whatever the client sent, so a reset or invite capability in a path segment reached the signed, append-only chain. Twenty-seven records across the middleware stack now carry the matched route instead.

Thirty-two reported defects are fixed in this release, among them an object-store `put` from a stream that could complete as an empty object after a retry, a download that kept a truncated file and reported success, a watcher whose process lifetime depended on which filesystem it was watching, and a cluster leader that appended to its own audit chain on a timer while completely idle. The documentation site also works on a phone: the navigation rail used to put over two thousand pixels of links above the content of every page.

items.title: Twenty namespaces have documentation pages
items.body: `b.createApp`, `b.objectStore`, `b.localDb`, `b.security`, `b.staticServe`, `b.safeEnv`, `b.safeJsonPath`, `b.mtlsEngine`, `b.fda21cfr11`, `b.tcpa10dlc`, `b.gdpr.ropa`, `b.nis2.report`, `b.incident.report`, `b.vaultWrap`, `b.vaultRotate`, `b.vaultPassphraseOps`, `b.vaultPassphraseSource`, `b.backupCrypto`, `b.backupManifest` and `b.backupBundle` each have a page, and each of their functions a signature, its options with defaults, the codes it raises and a worked example. Among them: that `b.createApp` installs nine middlewares without being asked and leaves `cors` and `rateLimit` for a deployment to configure; that `b.localDb.thin` fixes five pragmas and refuses a config naming any of them; that a backup's per-file subkey is bound to the file's path, so a blob moved inside a bundle stops decrypting; and that `b.mtlsEngine` picks its signature algorithm by generating a key and signing a certificate with it rather than by reading a capability flag, while the separate `canVerifyInTls` is what answers the handshake question.

items.title: A vault rotation's verification bounds reach the verification
items.body:
`b.vaultRotate.rotate` accepts `sampleMin` and `samplePercent` and did not pass either to the verification it runs over the staged copy, so an operator asking for a wider sample received the default five rows or one percent per table while believing the staged rotation had been checked more closely. Both are forwarded now. `tables` is not: it narrows what the rotation re-seals, and scoping the verification to the same subset would stop it reading the tables the rotation skipped, which is the one case that loses data at cutover. A sealed row left under the retired keypair still refuses the rotation with `vault-rotate/verify-failed`.

Both bounds are also checked before the staging directory is created. A `sampleMin` of `0` was refused after the directory existed, so the corrected retry then died on `vault-rotate/staging-exists` and the operator had to clear the directory by hand first.

items.title: A certificate's DNS subject alternative names are validated
items.body:
`b.mtlsEngine.signClientCert` and `b.mtlsEngine.packageP12` treated every `sans` entry that was not recognized as an IP address as a DNS name and wrote it into the certificate, so `"not a host !!!"` produced a certificate carrying an identity no peer can match, failing later at the handshake where the cause is hard to find. Only a value explicitly prefixed `IP:` was ever refused.

A DNS name is now checked before issuance: 1 to 253 octets, in labels of 1 to 63 letters, digits, `-` or `_`, each label starting and ending with a letter, digit or `_`, with an optional single leading `*` label. Anything else raises `mtls-engine/bad-san` naming the value. An entry that is not a string is refused too: a `null` or a port number left by a configuration placeholder was coerced and became the DNS name `"null"` or `"8443"`, both of which are valid labels. For `usage` `server` or `both` with no `sans`, the common name becomes the one DNS name and is held to the same rule, so a common name that survives normalization but cannot be a hostname, such as one made only of dots, is refused instead of issued.

A call that was issuing a usable certificate is unaffected. A call that was issuing an unusable one now raises. Underscores are accepted, since internal certificate authorities use them.

items.title: An incident stage records a copy of the fields it was filed with
items.body:
`b.incident.report`'s stage records kept the caller's own options object, so mutating or reusing it after filing changed what the record said had been filed, including the payload a `persist` sink had already received. A stage now stores a structured copy; `onStage` still receives the object as given.

The copy holds the data rather than the classes around it. Dates, Maps, Sets and cycles survive, a `Buffer` comes back as a `Uint8Array` over the same bytes, and a value whose `toJSON` lives on its prototype comes back as a plain object, so serializing the record can differ from serializing what was passed: pass plain data for anything a filing will be rendered from. A payload holding something that cannot be copied at all, such as a function, is kept by reference rather than emptied, since losing a filing's contents is worse than sharing the object.

items.title: A NIS2 stage filed while the CSIRT endpoint was down can be submitted again
items.body:
`b.nis2.report` records a stage against the directive's deadline and then POSTs the envelope, so a filing lands on time even when the CSIRT endpoint is unreachable. The call reported that as `submitted: false`, but the stage was filed and calling it again raised `incident-report/stage-already-filed`, leaving the operator with a record saying the stage was filed and no way to send it.

`resubmit(incidentId, stage)` re-POSTs the envelope for an already-filed stage and leaves the deadline record untouched; `stage` is `early-warning`, `notification` or `final`. It sends the fields as the stage record holds them, and a third argument replaces them for a report corrected in the meantime. A stage outside those three raises `nis2-report/bad-stage`, an unknown incident `nis2-report/unknown-incident`, and a stage not yet filed `nis2-report/stage-not-filed`.

items.title: A RoPA activity cannot be updated into an invalid one
items.body:
`b.gdpr.ropa`'s `update` validated only a changed `legalBasis`, so a patch clearing `name`, `purposes` or `dataCategories` was applied and the register exported an activity missing a field Article 30 §1 requires. `update` now validates the merged record, raising `gdpr-ropa/missing-field` or `gdpr-ropa/bad-legal-basis` and leaving the stored activity alone.

A required field is missing when it is `undefined` or `null`, raising `gdpr-ropa/missing-field`. A field that is present but unusable raises `gdpr-ropa/bad-field`: `name` has to be a non-empty string, and `purposes` and `dataCategories` non-empty arrays of names. A record stored with `purposes: 42` used to reach the Markdown export and throw an uncoded `TypeError` from `(e.purposes || []).join(", ")`. `id` keeps its own `gdpr-ropa/bad-id`, and `legalBasis` its `gdpr-ropa/bad-legal-basis`, which names the six bases.

A stored activity is frozen, with `purposes` and `dataCategories` copied and frozen as well, and that frozen record is what `register`, `update`, `get` and `list` answer with. The register previously kept the caller's object and handed it back, so clearing the array passed to `register`, or assigning to a field of the returned record, put an activity the validation had refused into the next export.

items.title: A manifest's aadBound is validated wherever a manifest is read
items.body: `b.backupManifest.validate` did not check `aadBound`'s type, so a manifest read off disk carrying `aadBound: "true"` passed, lost the field on the next `serialize`, and was restored as though the bundle were not AAD-bound. That surfaced as a decryption failure during the restore rather than a refusal of the manifest. `validate` now requires a boolean whenever the field is present, which `create`, `serialize` and `parse` all run.

items.title: A truncated backup ciphertext is refused before the key derivation
items.body: `b.backupCrypto.decryptWithKey` and `b.backupCrypto.decryptWithPassphrase` refused a buffer only at or below the 24-byte nonce, so a value of 25 to 39 bytes cleared the check, cost a full Argon2id derivation, and failed as `backup-crypto/decrypt-failed`. A sealed value needs the nonce and the 16-byte Poly1305 tag, so anything under 40 bytes now raises `backup-crypto/bad-input` first. `b.backupCrypto.TAG_BYTES` and `b.backupCrypto.MIN_SEALED_BYTES` are exported alongside `NONCE_BYTES`.

items.title: A vault passphrase from the environment can be asked to drop its trailing newline
items.body:
`b.vaultPassphraseSource.fromFile` strips trailing CR and LF and `fromEnv` does not, so a secret delivered through a shell heredoc or a `$(cat file)` reaches the two sources differently. The page said `fromEnv` trimmed; it never has.

`fromEnv({ trimTrailingNewlines: true })` makes it strip them. The default stays off: turning it on changes the derived key, so a vault sealed through this source from a value ending in a newline stops opening. Set it on a new vault, or re-seal an existing one with `b.vaultPassphraseOps.rotate` first. A value that is nothing but newlines is refused when trimming is on rather than read as an empty passphrase, and an interior newline is part of the passphrase either way.

items.title: The wrapping-key salt bound is enforced where the key is derived
items.body: The sealed-file format accepts a salt of 8 to 64 bytes, and `b.vaultWrap.buildHeader` enforced that while `b.vaultWrap.deriveWrappingKey` did not. A direct caller could derive a wrapping key under a 65-byte salt, which `buildHeader` would then refuse to record, and a salt shorter than 8 bytes surfaced as a native `ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` from Argon2 rather than the format's own refusal. Both now raise `vault-wrap/bad-salt`, from one check that `buildHeader` shares.

items.title: A vault rotation's remaining bounds are checked before it claims the staging directory
items.body:
`rowBatchSize` was read without validation and reached the SQLite `LIMIT` bind only after the staging directory had been created and filled, so a non-integer value failed partway through and the corrected retry then died on `vault-rotate/staging-exists`. It is validated with `sampleMin` and `samplePercent`, before anything is written.

The list options are checked too, each in the calls that read it: `tables` in all three of `rotate`, `verify` and `validateSchemaMatch`, and `infraColumns` in `validateSchemaMatch`. A value that is not an array of names was silently ignored, so an operator who wrote `infraColumns: "audit_log"` instead of a list received drift errors on the column they meant to allowlist and no way to turn them off. Each now raises `vault-rotate/bad-opt`.

Two options `rotate` never read have left its page: `db`, which `rotate` does not take because it decrypts the database file into staging and opens its own handle, and `infraColumns`, which only the schema check reads. `vault-rotate/no-db` is raised by `verify` and was never raised by `rotate`.

items.title: A boolean option given a non-boolean is refused instead of read as a default
items.body:
Across the namespaces documented in this release, a boolean option was read as `=== true`, `!== false` or for truthiness, so a configuration file deserialized into the string `"false"`, a `0` or a `null` quietly took the default instead of being refused. Each is now checked where it is used.

Two of them failed open, which is the direction that matters. `b.vaultPassphraseOps.seal`'s `keepPlaintext` was read with `!!`, so `"false"` was truthy and left the unencrypted vault key on disk while the call reported it deleted; it now raises `vault-passphrase/bad-opt`. `b.safeEnv.readVar`'s `strip` was read as `=== true`, so a non-boolean left the variable in `process.env` for every child process the deployment starts; it now raises `env/bad-opt`.

`b.createApp`'s eleven `middleware` keys are the widest change: each is `false`, `true` or that middleware's options object, and anything else raises. A `csrf: "false"` previously read as neither `false` nor an object, so the middleware came off without the `app.middleware.disabled` audit event that records a deliberate opt-out. The rest raise their own module's bad-option code: `b.backupManifest.create`'s `aadBound`, `b.backupBundle.create`'s `sign` and `signOptional`, `b.incident.report.createDeadlineClock`'s `audit` and `autoStart`, `b.localDb.thin`'s `audit`, `b.tcpa10dlc.recordConsent`'s `audit`, `b.security.assertProduction`'s `ntpStrict` and `allowDpiTrust`, and `b.mtlsEngine.signClientCert`'s `sans` when it is not an array. `b.incident.report.create`'s `audit` takes `false`, `true` or a configuration object such as `{ sink: yourAudit }`, and refuses a string or a number.

Each check runs before the work it guards: `b.backupBundle.create` refuses a malformed signing option before claiming the output directory rather than after encrypting every file, `b.safeEnv.readVar` refuses a malformed `strip` before reading and consuming the variable, and `b.createApp` refuses a malformed middleware key before the vault, the database and the job consumers start.

items.title: Every documented option of b.safeEnv.load is checked before the file is opened
items.body:
A malformed option read as its default instead of being refused. `allow: "KEY"` instead of `allow: ["KEY"]` died on an uncoded native `TypeError` from `.map()`, and `applyToProcess: "true"` was read as `false`, so the call reported a successful load while writing nothing to `process.env`. `allowOverwrite`, `audit`, `snapshotPath` and `expected` behaved the same way.

Each is now checked before the file is read, raising `env/bad-opt`: `applyToProcess`, `allowOverwrite`, `rejectUnknown` and `audit` must be booleans, `allow` an array of names, `snapshotPath` a non-empty string, and `expected` a plain object.

The `expected` schema's entries are checked at the same point. An entry is an object, its `type` is `string`, `number`, `boolean` or `json`, and its `sensitivity` is a non-empty string, each raising `env/bad-schema`; a non-boolean `required` raises `env/bad-opt`. `expected: { PORT: null }` previously passed and then threw an uncoded `TypeError` while reading the entry, and an unknown `type` on a key the file happened not to carry was never reached at all.

items.title: An object store built without a config refuses with a code
items.body: `b.objectStore.buildBackend()` called with no config threw a bare `Error`, so a caller catching by code could not catch it, while the same mistake against `b.objectStore.bucketOps.create()` raised `objectstore/bad-opt`. Both now raise `objectstore/bad-opt`. The message is unchanged in substance and the error still extends `Error`, so a `catch` that does not inspect the code behaves as before. `protocol` itself remains required: omitting it raises `protocol-dispatcher/missing-protocol` rather than selecting a backend nobody named.

items.title: The undocumented-namespace report no longer drops what it cannot locate
items.body: `find-missing-pages` resolved a namespace to a file by trying `lib/<namespace>.js`, its kebab-case spelling, and `lib/<namespace>/index.js`, and returned early when none existed. The namespace left the report with it, so twenty undocumented namespaces read as documented and the run reported that every one was covered. It now resolves the namespace through the export map in `index.js`, which answers with the implementing file whether the namespace sits in a subdirectory, is re-exported through a barrel, or is wrapped in an object literal, and it falls back to the filename conventions after that. A namespace that still cannot be placed is reported with no file rather than skipped.

items.title: A middleware that calls next(err) stops the request
items.body: `b.router` invoked each `use()` middleware with a `next` callback and ignored the argument it was given. A middleware reporting failure the documented way, `next(err)`, was read as if it had called `next()`, so the request continued to the route handler and the response was produced as though the check had passed. Any authentication, authorization or CSRF middleware written to that contract was advisory: it could log a refusal and still serve the request. `next(err)` now raises the error into the router's error path, which runs `onError` and answers with the failure status, and `next()` alone still continues the chain. A route handler declared with three parameters is treated the same way, and one that returns without calling `next` no longer falls through to a second response. Operators running a middleware that passes an error should expect requests it refuses to stop being served; a middleware that passed an error by mistake will now surface as a failing request rather than a silent log line. `b.testing.request` routed its own failures past the application's `onError`, which is why nothing caught this, and it now dispatches through the same handler the server uses.

items.title: Thirty-nine audit rows that were documented but never written now reach the chain
items.body: `b.audit` requires an action to be `namespace.verb[.qualifier]` with each segment lowercase, and requires the namespace to be registered. `safeEmit` caught that refusal and returned, which was indistinguishable from its documented contract for a sink on the request path. Together those two behaviors hid a class of missing evidence: thirty-nine emit sites across nineteen files passed an action the validator refuses, so the call reported success, raised nothing, and wrote no row. Among them are the rows that record an operator turning a scanner off, `fileupload.content_safety.disabled` and `staticserve.content_safety.disabled`, the backup envelope key rotation record auditors ask for, `backup.key_rotated`, the 0-RTT decisions `tls.zero_rtt.accepted`, `tls.zero_rtt.refused` and `tls.zero_rtt.replayed`, every differential-privacy budget decision in `b.ai.dp`, every quota decision in `b.ai.quota`, and the credential lifecycle of `b.auth.sdJwtVc`. Each of the thirty-four distinct actions is renamed to one b.audit accepts, and the seven namespaces they need, `apiencrypt`, `bodyparser`, `cms`, `fileupload`, `gatecontract`, `staticserve` and `vendordata`, are registered. The renames are `backup/key-rotated` to `backup.key_rotated`, `auditTools.purge.denied` to `audit.purge.denied`, `cms.signedData.encoded` and `cms.envelopedData.encoded` to `cms.signed_data.encoded` and `cms.enveloped_data.encoded`, `fileUpload.contentSafety.disabled` and `fileUpload.filenameSafety.disabled` to `fileupload.content_safety.disabled` and `fileupload.filename_safety.disabled`, `gateContract.posture.unmapped` to `gatecontract.posture.unmapped`, `mail.serverRegistry.method_dispatch` and `mail.serverRegistry.experimental_registration` to `mail.server_registry.*`, `body-parser.error` and `body-parser.multipart.file_rejected` to `bodyparser.*`, `pqcagent.reloadCerts` to `pqcagent.reload_certs`, `staticServe.contentSafety.disabled` to `staticserve.content_safety.disabled`, `vendor-data.boot_verify_deferred` to `vendordata.boot_verify_deferred`, the `tls.0rtt.*` actions to `tls.zero_rtt.*`, `ai/capability-routed`, `ai/capability-fallback` and `ai/capability-no-candidate` to `ai.capability.routed`, `ai.capability.fallback` and `ai.capability.no_candidate`, `dp/budget-exhausted` and `dp/budget-consumed` to `ai.dp.budget_exhausted` and `ai.dp.budget_consumed`, `ai/quota-applied` and `ai/quota-exceeded` to `ai.quota.applied` and `ai.quota.exceeded`, `auth.sdJwtVc.*` to `auth.sd_jwt_vc.*`, `dora.incident.draftFinal` to `dora.incident.draft_final`, and `apiEncrypt.session.*` to `apiencrypt.session.*`. No stored row carries an old name, because none was ever written, so there is nothing to migrate; a dashboard or alert built on one of these strings was matching nothing and should be pointed at the new one. `b.pqcAgent`'s reload row had a second fault on top of the spelling: the emit called a method on the `lazyRequire` getter rather than on the module, which raised a `TypeError` into the same silent catch. Five further actions were renamed in source without changing what is recorded, because `safeEmit` rewrites a hyphen to an underscore before storing: `cert.challenge-cleanup`, `cert.renew-failed`, `cert.ocsp.refresh-failed`, `mail.send.deliver.dsn-failed` and `webhook.dispatcher.dead-letter` were already being written under their underscored names, and the source now spells them the way they are stored. The EventEmitter event `cert.renew-failed`, which is a different surface, keeps its name.

items.title: b.audit.refusedActions() reports an action that was not recorded
items.body: `safeEmit` absorbs a failing sink on purpose, and it absorbed a refused action the same way, so a primitive emitting a misspelled action reported success and wrote nothing. The two are not the same kind of failure: a sink being down is a runtime condition, while an action the validator refuses is a defect in the emitting code that will drop every row on that path for the life of the process. A refused action is now logged once, counted as the observability event `audit.action_refused`, and listed by `b.audit.refusedActions()` as `{ action, attempts }`. A non-empty list means rows an operator was told to expect are not being written, and the remedy is in the message: register the namespace with `b.audit.registerNamespace`, or correct the action. Nothing about the hot path changes, the call still never throws, and a legal action is unaffected. `b.middleware.botDisclose` builds every row it writes from `auditAction`, so a prefix b.audit would refuse now fails at mount with `bot-disclose/bad-opt` rather than silently recording nothing. The register reported three more namespaces whose rows were going nowhere: `b.guardSql.gate` composed its served, audited and refused decisions under a camelCase namespace, and the `fsm` and `worm` namespaces were never registered, so every state transition and every WORM lock, release and expiry row was refused. The SQL gate now writes under `guardsql`, matching the `guardfilename` namespace the filename guard uses, and all three namespaces are registered.

items.title: BLAMEJS_VENDOR_DATA_PUBKEY_FINGERPRINT can pin the vendored-data signing key
items.body: Setting the variable to the correct fingerprint stopped the framework from loading. The comparison called `timingSafeEqual` on a `lazyRequire` getter instead of on the crypto module, so it raised a `TypeError` during the boot-time verification: a correct pin failed to boot, and a wrong pin produced that same `TypeError` rather than the mismatch refusal, which left the control unable to do the one thing it exists for. The comparison is now a constant-time hex compare. A correct pin boots, a wrong one refuses with `vendor-data/operator-fingerprint-mismatch`, a malformed one refuses with `vendor-data/operator-fingerprint-bad-shape`, and leaving the variable unset is unchanged.

items.title: A settled request releases its body instead of holding it until timeoutMs
items.body: `b.httpClient.request` added an abort listener to the request's signal and never removed it; `removeEventListener` did not appear in the file. Node keeps a signal from `AbortSignal.timeout()` alive until its timer fires while a listener is attached, and that listener's closure holds the options, so every request body stayed reachable for the whole of `timeoutMs` after the response had arrived. Measured against an object store with `timeoutMs: 120000`: all forty 16 MiB part buffers of a completed 640 MiB upload were still referenced, and four 8 MiB single-part bodies outlived their calls. The listener is now detached when the request settles, on both the HTTP/1.1 and the HTTP/2 path. In stream mode the release waits for the response body to end, and an HTTP/2 stream is bidirectional, so a server that answers in full before reading the request body left an upload still in flight when the response ended. The release now waits for the request to finish as well, and a five-chunk body sent to such a server arrives whole instead of as its first chunk. A buffered response is the same case with a `Buffer` body, which has no `end` event, so the cancellation listener came off as soon as the response was complete and neither the caller's signal nor `timeoutMs` could still reach the upload it left running. Both the buffered and the streamed completion now hold cancellation until the request finishes. A rejection is the third way a call completes, and it detached cancellation without ending the request, so an HTTP/1.1 server answering 413 before the body finished left the upload running with nothing able to stop it. A rejection now destroys a request whose body has not finished.

items.title: A streamed object-store put is not retried into an empty object
items.body: `b.objectStore.buildBackend` wraps `put` in `b.retry.withRetry`, and a retry called `put` again with the same readable. The source has already ended when the failure lands on the last part, on the only part of a source smaller than `partSizeBytes`, or on the completion call, so the next attempt read nothing: the backend uploaded a zero-byte part, completed the upload, and `put` resolved `{ size: 0 }`. The key held an empty object and the caller was told it had succeeded. A `put` whose body is a stream now gets one attempt and its failure reaches the caller. A Buffer or string body is replayable and is still retried.

items.title: getStream reads an object as it arrives rather than buffering it whole
items.body: `getStream()` on the sigv4, GCS, Azure Blob and HTTP PUT backends was built on the buffered `get()`: it awaited the whole response and then yielded it as one chunk. The first byte reached the caller only after the last byte arrived from the store, an object up to the 1 GiB get cap was held in memory in full, and every concurrent read held its own copy. The local backend already streams, and its `get()` refuses an object over 64 MiB with a message telling the caller to use `getStream()`, which on a remote backend read the whole object anyway. Each remote backend now issues its signed request in stream mode and hands the body through, so the bytes flow as they arrive and a failure part-way reaches the consumer as a stream error.

items.title: A truncated download is refused, and a failed transfer is retryable
items.body: `b.httpClient.downloadStream` hashed whatever arrived and renamed it onto `dest`. A body that ends early, which is the shape a canceled HTTP/2 stream takes because the readable side ends without an error, therefore landed as a complete file and the call resolved unless `expected` was set. The byte count is now compared with the declared `Content-Length` and a short body raises `http-client/truncated-body` with no file left at `dest`. The failure classification was wrong too: the error was built by a helper that marks every error permanent and stamps it with the response status, so a reset part-way through a body arrived as permanent with `statusCode: 200`. `b.retry.isRetryable` answered false on both counts and a `b.circuitBreaker` did not count the failure, while the same reset through a buffered `request` was retryable. A transfer that fails part-way is now reported as transient. The same length check guards the `getStream` of a backend built with `b.objectStore.buildBackend`, and a declared length does not always describe the message body: RFC 7230 section 3.3.2 lets a 304 carry the `Content-Length` of the selected representation, and a 304 carries no body. A conditional `getStream` that the store answered with a 304 was failing as `objectstore/truncated-body`. The check now skips every status that carries no body, 1xx, 204, 205 and 304, along with a `HEAD` or `CONNECT` response.

items.title: A watcher keeps the process alive under either backend, and its poll walk yields
items.body: `fs.watch` holds the event loop open on some platforms and the poll backend's interval was unref'd, so a program whose only work was watching kept running on a local disk and exited immediately on a bind mount, an NFS or an SMB mount, which is exactly where `mode: "auto"` picks poll. Lifetime now comes from one handle the watcher owns, so it is the same under either backend and on every platform, and `close()` releases it. The poll walk also ran `readdirSync` and `statSync` over the whole tree on the event loop from a `setInterval`, which measures each interval from the start of the previous tick: once a walk outlived `pollIntervalMs` the walks ran back to back and nothing else in the process got the loop. A `stat` is slowest on the FUSE, 9p, virtiofs, NFS, SMB and vboxsf mounts that `"auto"` selects poll for, and `pollMaxFiles` allows 50,000 entries. The walk now yields between directories and the next one is timed from the end of the last. `mode: "auto"` is documented, having been accepted but described nowhere.

items.title: A second log rotation in the same second keeps both archives
items.body: The local log sink named its archive from a timestamp with one-second resolution, so a second rotation inside the same second renamed the active file onto the name the first had taken and the gzip write replaced its `.gz`: the records in the first archive were gone, with nothing reporting it. A suffix is added until the name is free. A rotation that cannot complete, because a reader holds the active file open without delete sharing, used to be retried on every record, and each attempt slept through the rename backoff on the event loop and then dropped the record. The record is written to the active file instead, which grows past `maxFileBytes` until the rename succeeds, and the next attempt waits out a cooldown.

items.title: An idle cluster leader stops appending to its own audit chain
items.body: A leader renews its lease about every twelve seconds. The renewal issues an external-db query, every external-db query emits `system.externaldb.query`, and with an external-db backend the audit chain lives in that same store, so an idle leader appended a signed row per renewal: roughly 2.6 million chain rows a year, each hashed into the chain and covered by a checkpoint, recording nothing an operator did. A query the framework issues against the store that holds the chain is bookkeeping, not evidence, so the lease provider's query helper runs inside the self-emit suppression the chain already uses for its own writes. The suppression sits on that one storage call rather than around a lease operation, because a scope that wraps an operation swallows every audit emission inside it. An external-db query an application makes is unaffected and is still recorded.

items.title: The router's failure line no longer writes a credential to the log
items.body: `b.router` wrote `err.message`, and for an error that is not a framework error the first five stack lines, straight through the boot logger. An error message often names a file or a storage key, and when that key is a share id or a token the value reached stderr twice, once in the message and once in the first frame. Both now pass through `b.redact.redactText`, which scrubs a credential embedded in free text and keeps the surrounding words, so the line still says what failed. The level also read only `isFrameworkError`, so an application error carrying a `retryAfter`, the shape that asks the caller to come back, was written at error level with frames for every refused request; it is now written below error level without frames. A 4xx refusal, a 5xx, and an error carrying no status are unchanged.

items.title: Twenty-seven more audit and log records carry the route instead of the request URL
items.body: A request target recorded as a field carries whatever the client sent: a reset or invite capability sitting in a path segment, and every query parameter. The audit chain is signed and append-only, so a capability written there stays written. The detector that guards this matched only fields named `url`, `originalUrl`, `requestUrl` and `fullUrl`, and twenty-two sites recorded `req.url` under the names `path` and `route` instead, across `b.auth.accessLock`, `b.middleware.aiActDisclosure`, `b.middleware.bearerAuth`, `b.middleware.botDisclose`, `b.middleware.dpop`, `b.middleware.hostAllowlist`, `b.middleware.idempotencyKey`, `b.middleware.requireAal`, `b.middleware.requireContentType`, `b.middleware.requireMethods`, `b.middleware.requireStepUp` and `b.middleware.tracePropagate`. Six more recorded the path with the query stripped, which still carries a capability in a path segment, in `b.middleware.apiEncrypt`, `b.middleware.botGuard`, `b.middleware.cors`, `b.middleware.rateLimit` and `b.middleware.requireAuth`. Every one now records `b.requestHelpers.resolveRoute(req)`, the matched route pattern, which `b.router` sets before it runs the middleware chain. Widening the detector to those two field names and to the query-stripped form found five further sites, in `b.graphqlFederation`, `b.mcp`, `b.middleware.csrfProtect`, `b.middleware.fetchMetadata` and `b.middleware.requestLog`, which are fixed the same way. An operator reading these records now sees `/invite/:token` where the raw target used to be, which also groups cleanly in a log aggregator.

items.title: A verification that could not run is not a failed backup bundle
items.body: `verifyBundle` on the storage `b.backup.bundleAdapterStorage` returns caught every error from the passphrase unwrap and answered with a failed verification. A gate refusal, `argon2/busy` or `argon2/queue-timeout`, is transient and means the check never ran, so `{ ok: false, errors: ["argon2/busy"] }` reported an intact bundle as bad, and `verifyAllBundles` counted the repository as damaged. Both now raise the refusal instead, so a caller can tell a bundle that failed to read from one that was never read, and retry.

items.title: b.backup.runInWorker can put its worker under the shared Argon2id bound
items.body: The shared Argon2id gate is adopted by passing `b.auth.password.gateHandle()` to a worker through `workerData` and reclaiming its permits from the worker's `exit` event, using the thread id read while the worker was alive. `runInWorker` creates the worker itself and returns only a promise, so a caller could do neither: the handle could not reach `workerData` except by hiding it in `args`, and `worker.threadId` was never exposed. A worker terminated at `timeoutMs` mid-derivation therefore kept the permit it held for the life of the process, and under a shared limit of one every later derivation waited or was refused. `shareArgon2Gate: true` passes the handle as `workerData.argon2GateHandle` and reclaims that worker's permits when it exits. It rejects with `backup/no-shared-gate` when the calling thread holds its own limit, since there is no shared gate to join.

items.title: An SSRF refusal carries its code in err.code whatever error class is passed
items.body: `b.ssrfGuard.checkUrl` builds every refusal through the error class the caller hands it, and built it message-first. That fits its own `SsrfError`, and inverts a class built by `b.frameworkError.defineClass`, whose constructor takes the code first. `b.wsClient` passes one of those, so a refused dial arrived with `err.code` holding the human-readable text and `err.message` holding `ssrf-guard/blocked-cloud-metadata`. A consumer matching `err.code.startsWith("ssrf-guard/")` missed every refusal, including the cloud-metadata block that `allowInternal` cannot override. The refusal is now built through the class's own `factory`, so both argument orders land correctly. The same disagreement ran the other way through `b.safeUrl`, which builds the class it is given code-first: `checkUrl` parses through it and passes `SsrfError`, so a malformed URL inverted on the default error class too. `b.safeUrl` now prefers the factory as well. A refusal that was already correct, such as one from `b.httpClient`, is unchanged.

items.title: b.httpClient.request refuses an option it does not read
items.body: The `downloadStream` and multipart-upload blocks list `http-client/bad-opts` among the refusals of `request()` that reach the caller, and `request()` had no option allowlist: a name it did not know was accepted and ignored. A misspelled `timeoutMs` therefore left the request with no wall-clock cap at all, which is the failure the option exists to prevent. `request()` now refuses an unknown option with `http-client/bad-opts` and names it. The allowlist covers every option the client reads, including the three redirect spellings `b.httpClient.pinnedClient` forwards. Enabling it found one such typo in the framework's own test suite, a `timeout: 4000` that had never been read.

items.title: An open circuit breaker admits one half-open probe and answers with a typed error
items.body: Both descriptions of the half-open state say one probe runs. `wrap()` tested only for the open state, so the first call after `cooldownMs` moved the breaker to half-open and every call that arrived while that probe was still in flight saw half-open and ran as well. Against `b.objectStore`, which runs `put`, `get`, `head`, `delete`, `list` and `listVersions` through its breaker, the whole queue went back to the store whose failures opened it, and concurrent successes each counted toward `successThreshold` so they could close it together. Half-open now admits exactly one probe and every other arrival fast-fails. The open-breaker error was also a plain `Error`, and the breaker recognized its own refusal by `isObjectStoreError`, a flag it set on every breaker whether or not it fronted an object store. The refusal is now `b.circuitBreaker.CircuitOpenError`, carrying `isCircuitOpenError: true`, which is the flag to match; `code: "CIRCUIT_OPEN"`, `permanent: false` and `isObjectStoreError` are unchanged through the pre-1.0 line. The `RetryError` export on `b.circuitBreaker` named a class `lib/retry.js` never defined, so the property was `undefined` and testing an error against it with `instanceof` raised a `TypeError` instead of answering. It is removed, and `CircuitOpenError` is the class to match. `reset()` left the half-open probe permit held, so a call still in flight when the reset ran kept it. After the breaker opened again, every recovery probe fast-failed as `CIRCUIT_OPEN` for as long as that call stayed pending, and a call that hangs never releases it. `reset()` now frees the permit, and a call that started before a reset no longer releases a permit it no longer holds, which previously took the counter below zero and admitted two concurrent probes.

items.title: b.vaultWrap.isUnreadableFile asks whether a sealed file could be read
items.body: Every `b.vaultWrap` parse failure carries a `vault-wrap/*` code, and five framework callers separate an unreadable sealed file from a rejected passphrase with a predicate that was private. An application calling `b.vaultWrap.unwrap` directly had to restate the list of parse codes, and that list grows with each new check. `b.vaultWrap.isUnreadableFile(err)` answers the same question. A passphrase rejection and a derivation refusal such as `argon2/cost-over-ceiling` both answer false: the file was read, and something else failed.

items.title: An integrity check that cannot run no longer condemns the database
items.body: `b.localDb.thin` ran `PRAGMA integrity_check` at open and read any error from it as corruption: the sqlite error was discarded, the open raised `localdb-thin/corrupt`, and under `recovery: "rename-and-recreate"` the file was moved aside and replaced with an empty one. The check can fail without the file being damaged. `SQLITE_TOOBIG` is the deterministic case, raised when `limits.length` is below the size of a value already stored, and `SQLITE_IOERR` and `SQLITE_NOMEM` arrive the same way, while ordinary queries on the connection still work. The check's three answers are now distinguished: it reports `ok`, it lists the damage it found, or it could not run. The third raises `localdb-thin/integrity-check-failed` and leaves the file in place under either recovery, after confirming the connection still answers an ordinary query. The sqlite error that led to the verdict is carried into the refusal and into the `localdb.thin.recovered` audit row, which previously recorded that a database had been replaced without recording why.

items.title: verifyVendorIntegrity refuses a manifest that would verify nothing
items.body: `b.configDrift.verifyVendorIntegrity` documents a hard failure for a missing `packages` map so an operator does not get a silent zero-files-checked pass. The shape test was `typeof manifest.packages !== "object"`, and `typeof null` and `typeof []` are both `"object"`. A null map reached `Object.keys` and threw a `TypeError` carrying no code; an array, an empty map, or a package declaring no files verified nothing and answered `ok: true`. `packages` must now be a non-null object with at least one package in it, and anything else raises `config-drift/vendor-manifest-shape`. A package that declares no files is reported as `<unverifiable-manifest-entry>`, the way a single entry carrying no hash already was, so a run that verified nothing never returns `ok: true`.

items.title: ntpCheck.bootCheck acts on the variable it tells the operator to set
items.body: When no server answered, `bootCheck` returned `ok: true` with a message ending `set BLAMEJS_NTP_REQUIRE_REACHABLE=1 to refuse the boot instead`, and read no environment variable. Only `b.db.init` acted on it, so a program calling `bootCheck` directly and logging the message told its operator to set a variable that changed nothing in the answer it got back. `bootCheck` now reads it: with the variable set to `1` an unanswered query answers `ok: false` with `severity: "fatal"`, and the result carries `unreachableReason` either way. `b.db.init` reads that verdict rather than re-reading the variable, and still raises `db/ntp-unreachable`. The refusal quotes the reason the clock could not be read instead of the warning text, which had the effect of telling the operator to set the variable that had just caused the refusal. Any value other than `1` leaves the warning as it was.

items.title: A breach record cannot be edited after it is opened
items.body: `b.breach.report` returned its own stored record from `open`, `get` and `list`, so a caller holding one could assign to any field after the register had validated it. Writing `closedAt`, or emptying `deadlines`, changed the register's view of a statutory clock, and the next roll-up read the edited value. Those methods now answer with a deeply frozen copy, and `fileNotice` remains the only way to record a filing. `b.incident.report` answered its `open`, `get`, `list` and `record*` calls with the stored record for the same reason and is sealed the same way, through the same copier, which is also what its `persist` hook now receives. `b.gdpr.ropa` already froze the activity it returns. Code that mutated a returned record to record a filing has to call `fileNotice`; under a strict-mode module an assignment to the frozen copy throws, and otherwise it is ignored. The copy preserves the binary payload types a filing carries: a `Date`, a `Buffer`, a typed array, a `DataView` and an `ArrayBuffer` each come back as a copy of the same type. A `DataView` previously raised a `TypeError` out of the copy after the filing had already been recorded, which left `get` and `list` throwing as well, and a bare `ArrayBuffer` was stored as an empty object. Each type test reads the value's internal slot rather than comparing a constructor, so a value built in another realm, which is what a `vm` context or a worker hands back, is copied as what it is instead of being read for keys it does not have. An own `__proto__` key, which a JSON-parsed filing can carry, is defined on the copy rather than assigned, so it stays data.

items.title: A lost WebSocket connection is reported when it is lost, and urlFor moves the whole dial
items.body: `b.wsClient` had no `end` or `close` listener on its socket, so a connection lost without a Close frame surfaced only when the pong deadline passed, up to `pingIntervalMs + pongTimeoutMs` later. It now reports `ws-client/connection-lost` as soon as the peer goes away, and that code is transient, so a reconnecting client retries on it. `urlFor` returned a new URL for each attempt but only the TCP target moved: the path, the query and the `Host` header still came from the URL passed to `connect()`, so a failover to a second endpoint asked it for the first endpoint's path. Every attempt now dials the URL `urlFor` returned, and the audit rows carry the host that was dialed. After `cancelReconnect()`, and on a second `close()`, the client emitted no `close` event at all and left the socket open when the peer did not close it; both now emit `close` once and end the socket.

items.title: A failed DNS query reports the failure it had
items.body: `b.network.dns.lookup` ran the A and AAAA queries, replaced a failure of either with an empty list, and reported an empty result as `dns/no-result`, which `DnsError` classifies as permanent. A DoH endpoint that timed out, or a DoT connection that was refused, therefore looked like a name that does not exist, and `b.retry` did not retry it. When both queries fail and no address was found, the first query's error is what reaches the caller. `home.arpa`, the name RFC 8375 reserves for home networks, and any single-label name were also missing from the local-form list, so the resolver sent them to the configured public DoH endpoint, which answers NXDOMAIN for them and learns the name. Both are local-form now and go to the system resolver, and the suffix test compares on a label boundary, so `nothome.arpa` is not read as a subdomain of `home.arpa`.

items.title: The Argon2id cost ceiling refuses a ceiling that would refuse every hash
items.body: The internal `costCeiling` setter checked less than the public one: it accepted an unknown option name, accepted an array, and accepted a ceiling below the cost a default derivation uses, which refuses every hash the module writes. All three are refused with `argon2/bad-ceiling`, and the message names the default it compared against; `null` still restores the default. The `b.auth.password` introduction said the gate bounds derivations across every caller in the process. It bounds the callers that pass it, which is what the text says now.

items.title: A proxy's HTML error page keeps its status in passthrough mode
items.body: `b.httpClient.encrypted` with `responseMode: "passthrough"` is documented to resolve a non-2xx response with its status, body and `ok: false`, and the client parsed every non-empty body as JSON before it looked at the mode. A reverse proxy's default error page is HTML, so an nginx 502 rejected with `api-encrypt/client-response-not-json`, `statusCode: 400` and `permanent: true`: the caller could not read the real status, `b.retry.isRetryable` answered false, and a `b.circuitBreaker` did not count the failure. A non-2xx body that is not JSON now resolves in passthrough mode with the response's own status and the body as text. A body over `maxDecryptedBytes` still refuses.

items.title: A refused WebSocket upgrade cannot take the process down
items.body: A socket that has been through an `upgrade` event belongs to the application, and Node has removed its own error handling from it by then. The upgrade refusals wrote a response and destroyed the socket without attaching an `error` listener, so a reset while that write was in flight emitted `error` on a socket nothing was listening to, which Node raises at the top level. Every upgraded socket now carries a listener that destroys it instead, applied before anything is written to it. The shutdown's HTTP phase also called `server.close()` alone, which stops accepting and then waits for the connections already open, so an idle keep-alive peer held the phase to its ten-second timeout and was left to reset; the phase now closes idle connections alongside `close()`.

items.title: The documentation site is usable on a phone
items.body: The navigation rail carries every concern group and every primitive, and below 768px it was laid out as a single column with the whole rail stacked above the content. On a 390px viewport that put 2367 pixels of links above the start of the page on `/csv`, so reading any page began with scrolling past the entire site index. The rail now collapses behind a `Browse the docs` disclosure at that width and the content starts 267 pixels down, with the logo and both search boxes still in view. The disclosure is CSS only, which keeps it working under the default content-security policy that blocks inline script, and the control it is driven by stays in the tab order so the rail opens from the keyboard. Navigation links and the two search inputs get a 44px minimum height for a finger, and a wide table scrolls inside its own box rather than widening the page. Nothing changes at desktop width: the three-column layout, the sticky rail and the on-this-page column are as they were, and the disclosure is not rendered at all.

items.title: The vendored Public Suffix List is refreshed to the 2026-10-07 snapshot
items.body: `lib/vendor/public-suffix-list.dat` carries the list published at `2026-10-07_07-28-19_UTC`, commit `3929462652695bad04f0a27afb600974014a3c8b`, re-signed and re-hashed in `lib/vendor/MANIFEST.json`. Upstream replaced twenty-seven explicit `replit.dev` entries with `*.replit.dev` and `*.teams.replit.dev`, so a registrable-domain lookup under `replit.dev` now resolves any subdomain rather than only the named ones. Everything that reads the list sees the change: `b.guardDomain`, cookie-domain checks and the public-suffix lookups in the request path.

items.title: The vendored PKI bundle is refreshed to 0.9.1
items.body: `lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` carries `@blamejs/pki` 0.9.1, with `lib/vendor/MANIFEST.json` re-hashed to match. The framework still ships zero npm runtime dependencies; this is the bundled copy the X.509, ASN.1/DER and CMS paths read. The two upstream releases it crosses are both hardening ones. A record the toolkit defaults for an omitted argument no longer inherits from `Object.prototype`, so a revocation deadline is measured against the toolkit's own clock rather than an inherited one, a report is held to the caps its caller passed, a signer signs with the identity its caller named, and a client reads the status, body and headers a server actually sent. `pki.smime.verify` and `pki.smime.decrypt` refuse an entity whose `Content-Type` declares one parameter twice or whose header area declares one field twice, since both readings are conforming and they differ, and one MIME entity is bounded at 1024 body parts, 1024 header lines and 256 `Content-Type` parameters, charged as the entity is scanned. The record `pki.smime.verify` returns no longer shares the buffer the caller passed in.

items.title: The progress-callback invoker is one primitive
items.body: `b.backupBundle`, `b.restoreBundle` and `b.vaultRotate` each carried a byte-identical helper that called the operator's `progressCallback` inside a try/catch. All three now call `b.safeAsync.safeInvoke`, which is the framework's drop-silent callback invoker. A callback that throws is still ignored, so a progress hook cannot fail a backup or a rotation.

items.title: An undocumented public namespace fails the test suite
items.body: The undocumented-namespace report ran only when someone invoked it and always exited zero. It is now asserted in the framework's own suite, which fails naming each public function-bearing namespace that carries no documentation, together with the file to put it in. The resolver is asserted separately against the namespaces whose files the old guess could not derive, so the mapping is held even while nothing is undocumented.
